title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 147
paragraphs: Such was his order, and he added this saying at the same time: if the spies had been put to death, the Greeks would not have learned beforehand how far beyond description his power was; and on the other hand, by killing three men they would not have done the enemy much damage. But when these men returned to Greece, he thought the Greeks, hearing of his might, would hand over their freedom to him of their own accord, before the expedition even took place; and in that case there would be no need for him to take the trouble of marching against them. This opinion of his is much like his way of thinking at other times. For when Xerxes was at Abydos, he saw grain ships from the Pontus sailing through the Hellespont on their way to Aegina and the Peloponnese. Those sitting beside him, on being told that the ships belonged to the enemy, were ready to capture them and looked to the king to see when he would give the word. But Xerxes asked where the men were sailing, and they replied, “Master, to your enemies, carrying grain to them.” He then said: “Are we not sailing to the same place ourselves, provided with grain as well as the other necessities? How then do these men wrong us, seeing that they are carrying provisions that will serve us?”
